stories.headline: Double Earthquakes Strike Venezuela Near Caracas, Buildings Collapse with Mass Casualty Risk
stories.summary:
Two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela in rapid succession on Wednesday afternoon, with a 7.2-magnitude quake followed just 39 seconds later by a stronger 7.5-magnitude tremor. The U.S. Geological Survey warned that "high casualties and extensive damage are probable and the disaster is likely widespread," estimating a 44% chance of more than 10,000 fatalities and a 30% chance of more than 100,000 deaths.

Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello confirmed on state television that buildings had collapsed in Caracas, with the neighborhoods of Los Palos Grandes and Altamira among the worst affected. The quakes were felt hundreds of kilometers away in neighboring Colombia, including the capital Bogotá, where some buildings were evacuated as a precaution. A tsunami warning was issued for Venezuela's coast and the islands of Aruba and Bonaire but was later cancelled.

The disaster struck on a national holiday in Venezuela commemorating the 1821 Battle of Carabobo, meaning more residents than usual were at home when the quakes hit. The USGS noted significant risks of secondary hazards including landslides and soil liquefaction. Multiple Venezuelan states were reported affected, including Trujillo, Yaracuy, Carabobo, Aragua, Miranda and the capital district.

Venezuela's infrastructure, already severely degraded after years of economic crisis, faces a formidable recovery challenge. Emergency services were placed on full alert as authorities began assessing the scope of damage across the affected regions.

stories.headline: Postmaster General Confirms USPS Will Withhold Mail Ballots in States Refusing to Share Voter Data
stories.summary:
Postmaster General David Steiner told a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Wednesday that the U.S. Postal Service will no longer deliver mail-in ballots in states that refuse to provide sensitive voter data to the federal government, in line with a proposed Trump administration rule. Steiner confirmed the policy would withhold absentee and mail ballot lists from states declining to comply with federal data-sharing demands.

The announcement came on the same day a federal appeals court ruled that Michigan is not obligated to hand over unredacted voter data to the Trump administration. A divided three-judge panel for the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals held that Title III of the 1960 Civil Rights Act does not authorize the Justice Department to compel the state to provide such information, setting up a potential legal conflict with the new postal policy.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that voter data sharing is necessary to ensure election integrity and that states refusing federal oversight may be concealing irregularities. Critics and voting rights advocates contend the policy is an unconstitutional coercion of states and would disenfranchise millions of voters who rely on mail ballots, particularly the elderly, disabled, and military personnel overseas.

The policy carries significant implications for November's midterm elections, as mail voting has expanded substantially in recent election cycles. Several states are expected to challenge the rule in court if it is formally adopted, adding to a growing body of election-administration litigation heading into the fall campaign season.

stories.headline: General Chris Donahue, Last U.S. Soldier Out of Kabul, to Retire Early in Latest Senior Military Departure Under Hegseth
stories.summary:
The U.S. Army confirmed Wednesday that General Chris Donahue, one of its most prominent senior officers, will retire early and leave his post as the top Army commander in Europe ahead of schedule. Donahue is historically notable as the last American soldier to depart Afghanistan in 2021 and previously led the Army's elite forces during deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan. He is the sixth Army three- or four-star officer to announce early retirement in roughly the past year and a half.

The departures follow a broader pattern under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, in which senior officers have been asked to resign, fired, or reassigned to lower-ranking commands. Jim McPherson, who served as Under Secretary of the Army during Trump's first term, described the situation as "a very distressing pattern," noting that officers are being removed without public explanation or formal cause, departing from longstanding military tradition.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that civilian leadership has both the legal authority and the responsibility to shape military leadership to align with policy priorities, and that the secretary of defense has wide discretion over officer promotions and assignments. Critics, including McPherson, warn that the absence of transparent justification fuels speculation that removals are politically motivated, which they argue undermines military morale, institutional trust, and readiness.

The loss of experienced commanders like Donahue — whose career spanned two decades of combat leadership — raises questions about continuity in key commands, particularly the Army's European posture amid the ongoing war in Ukraine and continued NATO commitments.

stories.headline: Update: Colombia Election Confirmed — Far-Right De la Espriella Declared Official Winner
stories.summary:
Colombian electoral authorities completed the legally binding vote verification Wednesday and confirmed Abelardo de la Espriella as the country's president-elect. The result ends days of uncertainty following a razor-thin initial count reported in earlier coverage. De la Espriella, a far-right candidate backed by former President Donald Trump, defeated his rival to succeed outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro.

De la Espriella has pledged to reverse Petro's foreign policy, including rebuilding diplomatic and economic ties with the United States and Israel, which deteriorated sharply under Petro's administration. The election represents a significant rightward shift for one of South America's largest and most strategically important nations.

The outcome is expected to have regional implications, potentially realigning Colombia's posture on trade, security cooperation, and Venezuela policy. The United States under the Trump administration had closely monitored the vote, with Trump's public backing of de la Espriella making Colombia a high-profile test case for U.S. influence in Latin American electoral politics.

stories.headline: French Woman Held Captive in Pakistan for 12 Years Rescued After Son Sneaks Out to Alert Police
stories.summary:
Pakistani police raided a home in Bara, a remote town in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, after one of the captive woman's sons managed to slip out and file a report with authorities. Officers discovered Sylvie Yasmina, a 54-year-old French national, and her five children confined to a cramped, dilapidated room, with visible bruises across their bodies. Her husband, a Pakistani national, was arrested on allegations of physical and mental abuse carried out daily over more than a decade.

Yasmina told police she had been effectively imprisoned since the family relocated from Australia to Pakistan in 2014, with no contact with the outside world since then. Three of her five children were born in Pakistan and had never been enrolled in school. Her two older children had also been denied education during the years of alleged captivity.

Yasmina and her children have been transferred to a women's shelter in Peshawar and are expected to return to France. Pakistani authorities said the husband had been residing illegally in Australia when he and Yasmina met, and the couple married in 2003 before eventually moving to Pakistan. The husband has not been publicly identified by police.

stories.headline: Commanding General of U.S. Army Forces in Europe and Africa Stepping Down at Hegseth's Request
stories.summary:
Gen. Christopher Donahue, the commanding general of U.S. Army forces in Europe and Africa and leader of NATO's Allied Land Command, will resign on July 2 after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth requested his retirement papers, the Army confirmed Wednesday. Donahue is among more than two dozen senior military leaders to leave or retire early under Hegseth's tenure as the defense secretary moves to reduce the number of generals and redirect resources toward enlisted ranks. His deputy, Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, will assume his duties after July 2.

Donahue is one of the most recognizable figures in recent U.S. military history, best known as the last American soldier to board a plane out of Afghanistan in August 2021, a moment captured in an iconic night-vision photograph. He commanded the 82nd Airborne Division during the chaotic Kabul evacuation, overseeing the airlift of roughly 124,000 Afghan civilians. His leadership of that operation drew bipartisan praise even as the broader withdrawal strategy was widely criticized.

The departure carries significant strategic weight given Donahue's role overseeing U.S. Army forces across the European and African theaters at a time of active conflict in Ukraine and ongoing NATO commitments. Critics of Hegseth's leadership purge argue that removing experienced commanders weakens American deterrence at a critical moment; supporters contend the Pentagon brass had grown bloated and insufficiently focused on warfighting readiness.

Hegseth ordered a new Pentagon investigation last year into the Afghanistan withdrawal, a probe that overlapped with Donahue's command responsibilities. The timing of his forced departure adds to a broader reshaping of the military's senior leadership under the Trump administration.

stories.headline: U.S. Forces Kill Senior ISIS Leader in Syria Airstrike, Centcom Announces
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday that a June 19 airstrike in northwestern Syria killed Ali Husayn al-'Ulaywi, a senior Islamic State leader. The strike is part of what Centcom described as ongoing U.S. efforts to disrupt and eliminate terrorist networks operating in the region. No American casualties were reported in connection with the operation.

The announcement comes as the United States maintains a residual military presence in Syria focused on counterterrorism operations against ISIS remnants, even as diplomatic attention is concentrated on the broader Middle East situation involving Iran and Israel. Senior ISIS figures have continued to operate in northwestern Syria despite years of U.S.-led coalition pressure against the group's territorial holdings.

Centcom did not provide details on al-'Ulaywi's specific role within the ISIS command structure or whether any other individuals were killed or wounded in the strike. The June 19 date of the operation means the announcement comes five days after the fact, a common practice for sensitive counterterrorism missions where operational security concerns delay public disclosure.

stories.headline: Camp Mystic Files for Bankruptcy Nearly a Year After Floods Killed 27
stories.summary:
Camp Mystic, the Texas all-girls Christian camp where catastrophic flooding on July 4, 2025 killed 25 girls and two teenage counselors, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization on Wednesday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in the Southern District of Texas. The camp listed debts exceeding $10 million against assets of between $100,001 and $500,000.

Families of the victims filed a lawsuit in November seeking more than $1 million in damages, alleging camp operators failed to take necessary protective measures as life-threatening floodwaters rose along the Guadalupe River. Legislative and court hearings exposed the camp's lack of detailed flood emergency planning and its reliance on poorly trained staff. Camp owner Richard Eastland also died in the flood, which killed at least 136 people in total along a several-mile stretch of the river.

The bankruptcy filing comes weeks after Camp Mystic reversed plans to reopen this summer following an outcry from victims' families and lawmakers. The camp had previously invited journalists and legislators to review safety improvements and argued that hundreds of families wanted to return, but ultimately abandoned reopening plans in April amid ongoing lawsuits and state investigations.

The filing raises questions about the ability of victims' families to recover damages through the civil court system, as the camp's significant debt-to-asset imbalance could limit payouts. Attorneys for Camp Mystic and the Eastland family had not responded to requests for comment as of Wednesday.

stories.headline: Kenya to Charge Students with Murder over Deadly School Dormitory Fire
stories.summary:
Kenyan prosecutors announced Wednesday they will charge eight students with 16 counts of murder each in connection with a May 28 dormitory fire at Utumishi Girls' School in Gilgil that killed 16 pupils and injured dozens more. The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions said it approved the charges following a forensic review of CCTV footage, student and staff interviews, and police investigation concluding the students were involved in planning and executing the arson by setting mattresses alight near an exit.

The fire tore through the upper floor of a dormitory housing 202 students, who were forced to flee through a single doorway after an emergency exit failed to open. The victims were aged between 15 and 18. Education Minister Julius Ogamba said preliminary findings indicated multiple safety breaches including dormitory overcrowding and a locked exit door. The eight suspects, who are minors, are being held in custody and are due to be formally charged in court on Friday in Naivasha.

The case has reignited a national debate about a long-running epidemic of school fires in Kenya, many attributed to arson by students protesting disciplinary measures or poor living conditions. The ODPP expressed concern over a recent rise in arson incidents at Kenyan schools and warned that those responsible would face full accountability. Just two years ago, at least 21 people died in a separate dormitory fire in central Kenya.

The decision to charge minors with murder reflects prosecutorial determination to respond to what officials described as a systemic and worsening problem. Safety advocates have repeatedly warned that overcrowding, locked exits, and non-compliance with fire regulations are creating deadly conditions across Kenya's boarding school system.

stories.headline: Record Quarter of World Cup Players Represent Nations Where They Were Not Born
stories.summary:
The 2026 FIFA Men's World Cup features the highest proportion of foreign-born players in the tournament's history, with nearly one quarter of all participating players representing nations other than their birth countries, according to analysis of official squad lists submitted to FIFA. Only eight of the 48 competing teams have no player born abroad, reflecting a structural shift in how elite football talent is identified, recruited, and nationalized.

The trend has produced striking cases: World Cup debutants Curacao have only one player born on the Caribbean island; Qatar has assembled players from 10 nationalities; and high-profile cases such as Bayern Munich winger Michael Olise, born in London, who chose to represent France through his mother's nationality. Among the United States squad, Antonee Robinson qualified through his American father despite being born in Milton Keynes, England.

The phenomenon has created unusual family dynamics, with four sets of brothers representing different nations in the same tournament — including Desire and Guela Doue (France and Ivory Coast) and Nico and Iñaki Williams (Spain and Ghana). The tournament has already seen France-born Ibrahim Mbaye score for Senegal against France, echoing the 2022 moment when Cameroon-born Breel Embolo scored for Switzerland against his birth nation.

Migration scholars say the pattern reflects broader global trends. Professor Gijsbert Oonk of Erasmus University noted that nearly 4 percent of the world's population now lives outside their birth country, a figure even higher among high-skilled workers and elite athletes. Research from Oxford University's Centre on Migration, Policy and Society shows the share of foreign-born World Cup players has risen sharply in recent cycles after decades of fluctuation.

stories.headline: Eight Antifa Members Sentenced to Collective 450 Years for Anti-ICE Riot in Which Officer Was Shot
stories.summary:
A federal judge sentenced eight people with alleged ties to Antifa to a combined 450 years in prison Tuesday for their roles in a July 4, 2025, riot outside an immigration detention center in Prairieland, Texas. Benjamin Hanil Song, described by prosecutors as the group's leader and convicted of attempted murder of a law enforcement officer, received 100 years; sentences for the remaining seven ranged from 30 to 70 years. The defendants were convicted on charges including rioting, use of weapons and explosives, providing material support to terrorists, and obstruction.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that the sentences demonstrated violent attackers of law enforcement and federal facilities would face "swift and uncompromising justice." The presiding judge called the July 4 assault "an assault on democracy." A ninth defendant is scheduled for sentencing on July 1, along with seven others who pleaded guilty before trial.

Defendants' families and supporters condemned the sentences as disproportionate. Song wrote in a statement that he fired his weapon because he believed an officer was about to shoot a protester; his mother disputed that he shot anyone and said he did not intend to harm anyone, according to the Associated Press. Advocacy groups for the defendants characterized the punishments as unduly harsh.

The case carries broad political significance. President Trump designated Antifa a domestic terrorist organization in 2025, and the Justice Department framed the convictions as part of a broader effort against what it described as a network seeking to overthrow the government and law enforcement. Critics on the left argued the sentences reflect an aggressive use of terrorism statutes against political protesters.

stories.headline: New Fed Chair Warsh Retreats From Decades of Transparency, Risking Higher Rates and Market Volatility
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over the central bank earlier this year, is sharply curtailing the Fed's communications with financial markets, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater transparency. At his first press conference last week, Warsh stripped the central bank's post-meeting statement of forward guidance — signals about future interest-rate moves — that markets had relied upon to anticipate Fed policy. His approach echoes that of former Chair Alan Greenspan, who died Monday at 100 and was the only predecessor Warsh praised at his swearing-in.

Analysts warn the shift carries tangible economic risks. Without clear Fed signals, bond and stock markets may swing more sharply, and borrowing costs for consumers and businesses could rise modestly — perhaps a quarter-point on mortgage rates, according to George Pearkes, global macro strategist at Bespoke Investment Group. Pearkes said forward guidance has historically "suppressed volatility and anchored market expectations," leading to lower borrowing costs.

Warsh has argued that markets have become too dependent on Fed direction and that such guidance is better reserved for financial crises or severe downturns. His philosophy represents a philosophical break from the approach of recent chairs, who moved toward greater openness in part at Congress's urging. The practical test will come at future Fed meetings as investors are left to interpret rate decisions without the roadmaps they have grown accustomed to.

The transition comes at a consequential moment, with inflation and the tariff-driven economic outlook already creating uncertainty. The Fed's independence has also been a source of tension with the Trump administration. How markets absorb Warsh's more opaque style in the coming months will be closely watched as a signal for whether reduced transparency measurably raises the cost of credit for households and businesses.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Claims Vandalism at Reflecting Pool, Says 13 Arrested or Cited — AP Finds Evidence Contradicts Account
stories.summary:
President Trump escalated his claims Tuesday that vandals deliberately damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, asserting on social media that six people had been arrested and seven cited for causing a "350-foot gash" in the freshly painted liner — though he provided no supporting evidence and said images would be released to prove his account. The $14-million rehabilitation project drained the century-old pool, painted its bottom a color Trump called "American flag blue," and became a focal point of preparations for the nation's 250th anniversary celebration next week.

The Associated Press, which verified events at the site, found that one man was arrested after briefly touching paint that was already peeling — he said he wanted to examine the new coating and released a still-attached chunk shortly after a park worker told him to stop. The U.S. Park Police and Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment on Trump's specific arrest claims. National Guard members and Park Police have been deployed around the pool's deck after Trump began blaming vandals over the weekend.

The pool has been beset by problems since its restoration, including persistent algae blooms and visible peeling of the new liner coating. Scientists and critics have pointed to the paint formula and application as contributing factors. Trump has consistently attributed the deterioration to deliberate sabotage, saying "somebody had to work very hard, probably in the dark of night, to create such a condition."

The episode has become politically charged ahead of July 4 celebrations. Supporters of the renovation defend it as a patriotic upgrade to a national landmark, while critics argue the project was rushed, poorly executed, and that unsubstantiated vandalism claims are being used to deflect accountability for a flawed renovation funded by taxpayers.

stories.headline: Update: France Confirms First Ebola Case in Europe as Congo Outbreak Surpasses 1,000 Infections
stories.summary:
France has confirmed its first case of Ebola, involving a doctor who returned from a humanitarian mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The physician was immediately admitted to a specialized medical facility and is reported to be in stable condition, according to the French health ministry. Authorities stressed the risk to the general public remains "very low" and are working to trace any contacts the doctor may have had.

The case marks the first confirmed Ebola infection on European soil, though an American doctor who tested positive in DRC was treated at a German hospital last month. The ongoing outbreak in DRC has now surpassed 1,000 infections and claimed more than 260 lives, with cases concentrated in the eastern provinces of Ituri, South Kivu, and North Kivu. Neighboring Uganda has also recorded 20 infections and two deaths.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, for which no approved vaccine currently exists, complicating containment efforts. The World Health Organization has warned that active conflict in eastern DRC, where the M23 rebel group controls large areas, is significantly hampering the public health response. Africa CDC and U.S. public health authorities have described the outbreak as having the potential to become one of the largest ever recorded.

France has established a dedicated monitoring system for aid workers returning from DRC and confirmed it is conducting contact tracing. The confirmation of a European case is likely to intensify pressure on international health bodies to accelerate response funding and logistics, particularly as previous U.S. foreign aid cuts — including USAID reductions — have been cited as hampering on-the-ground containment work in DRC.

stories.headline: Update: European Heatwave Intensifies as France Records Hottest June Day Ever, 40 Dead
stories.summary:
France recorded its hottest average June day since records began on Tuesday, with a mean temperature of 29.8°C and peaks of 44.3°C in the Landes region. Red heat alerts have been extended to 58 of France's regions, with 31 additional regions under orange alert. The extreme heat has caused the country's first major heat-related power outage, leaving around 68,000 homes in Brittany without electricity, with full restoration not expected until end of day Wednesday.

At least 40 people have drowned in heatwave-related incidents in France since last Thursday, according to the French prime minister. Temperatures of 39–43°C are forecast across much of western France, from Paris to Brittany, through the weekend. The Louvre museum in Paris announced it would close two hours early each day through Saturday due to the heat in its historic building.

The heatwave is spreading across western Europe, with orange danger alerts issued for the Netherlands, while Germany is forecast to see temperatures reach 40°C over the weekend. Severe heat warnings have been extended to Poland, Croatia, and Hungary for later in the week. A major wildfire in the Maine-et-Loire region required more than 150 firefighters before being brought under control overnight.

The new material developments — France's record temperatures, the 40 drowning deaths, the mass power outage, and the heatwave's spread into northern and eastern Europe — represent a significant escalation from prior coverage. French labor minister Jean-Pierre Farandou said the country is "in the process of finding out we've become a hot country." Some relief is forecast from Friday, accompanied by risks of flash flooding and large hail from thunderstorms.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Drone Strike Blacks Out Sevastopol as Crimea Faces Fuel Shortages
stories.summary:
Ukrainian drones struck the main power substation of Sevastopol overnight, knocking out electricity across Russia's largest occupied city in Crimea. Moscow-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhayev warned some areas would remain without power until Wednesday evening and placed all emergency services on full alert. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces commander confirmed the attack was part of a broader overnight operation targeting 48 military sites.

The attack comes as Crimea is already under severe strain from a Ukrainian campaign to isolate the peninsula. All petrol sales have been suspended by Russian-installed authorities and reserved largely for government services, while panic-buying of basic goods has been reported in local shops. Kyiv has also targeted key bridges and road links connecting Crimea to mainland Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's defense ministry said it destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine's air force reported intercepting 95 of 101 Russian drones launched against Ukrainian territory. The intensified Ukrainian campaign against Crimean infrastructure is part of Kyiv's broader strategy of damaging Russian energy revenues and compelling Moscow to engage in negotiations. Sevastopol is a strategically vital port city and serves as a key logistical hub for Russian forces in the region.

Explosions were also reported in Bakhchisarai, Kerch, and near Mount Ai-Petri, where a Russian Aerospace Forces communications battalion is based. The strikes mark an escalation in Ukraine's pressure on occupied Crimea and come as fighting continues on multiple fronts in eastern Ukraine, where Russian troops have infiltrated the strategic city of Kostyantynivka.

stories.headline: Alibaba Sues Pentagon to Fight Military Blacklist That Would Sever U.S. Legal and Business Ties
stories.summary:
Chinese tech and e-commerce giant Alibaba has filed a lawsuit in a California federal court challenging its placement on the Pentagon's "1260H" blacklist, which designates companies deemed to be linked to China's military. The U.S. Department of Defense placed Alibaba on the list on the grounds that its compliance with Chinese technology regulators makes it effectively an arm of the Chinese military-civil fusion apparatus. Alibaba called the designation "arbitrary and capricious" and said it has "no basis in fact or law."

The practical stakes are acute: starting June 30, the Pentagon is legally barred from doing business with blacklisted firms, and — critically — the restriction extends to any U.S. contractor that shares a lobbyist or law firm with a blacklisted entity. Alibaba argues this effectively forces its American legal and political advisers to sever ties in order to protect their own defense contracts, stripping the company of representation in Washington at the precise moment it needs to fight back. The company says it previously sought a meeting with the DoD to present evidence of its U.S. economic contributions but received no response and no hearing before being designated.

Alibaba pushed back on the military affiliation claim, noting that all multinationals operating in China — including American companies — must comply with local regulations, and that none of its independent board members has any military ties. The company's platforms, it said, are built for retail and cloud computing, not defense or intelligence purposes. The DoD declined to comment on the litigation.

The case is part of a broader U.S. government effort to restrict Chinese technology firms: Baidu, BYD, and Nio are among other major companies recently added to the expanded blacklist. The outcome could set an important legal precedent for how U.S. regulators may designate foreign companies under national security statutes and how those companies may challenge such designations in court.
